# The Average Man Does Not Exist

In 1950, the United States Air Force had a problem it could not name. Its pilots were crashing. Not in combat — in training, in routine flights, in machines that behaved exactly as designed. Sometimes a dozen men died in a week. The investigations reached for the usual vocabulary: pilot error, poor judgment, failure to anticipate. But the crashes did not cluster around the incompetent. Good pilots were flying perfectly serviceable aircraft into the ground, and the phrase "pilot error" began to look less like an explanation than a place to stop asking questions.

Eventually someone thought to measure the cockpits, and then to measure the men. The cockpits had been designed in the 1920s around the average dimensions of that era's pilots: seat depth, the distance from seat to pedals, the height of the windscreen, the reach to the throttle. Every one of those measurements was a reasonable number. Together they described a man who could fly comfortably. The Air Force suspected that the pilots of 1950 might have drifted from that man — that they were taller, perhaps, or longer in the arm — and that a new average was needed.

So a researcher named Gilbert Daniels measured 4,063 pilots across more than a hundred dimensions, then narrowed to the ten that mattered most for fitting into a seat. He computed the middle range of each. And then he asked the question nobody had asked, which was not *what is the average pilot* but *how many pilots are average*.

Zero. Not one of four thousand and sixty-three men fell in the middle range on all ten measurements. Narrow it to three dimensions and fewer than four percent qualified. The average pilot was not rare. He was fictional. He had never existed, not in 1926 and not in 1950, and the cockpits had been built for a ghost the whole time.

What followed was one of the quiet revolutions of the twentieth century, and it did not involve any new theory of the human being. It involved adjustable seats. Sliding rails, movable pedals, repositionable straps. The cockpit stopped knowing what a pilot was and started letting each pilot tell it. Crash rates fell. The innovation was not a better guess about the human body. It was the abandonment of guessing.

I find this story almost unbearably good, and the reason is not the punchline. It's the fact that the mistake had been sitting there for thirty years, invisible, protected by a number that seemed obviously sensible. Nobody had been careless. Everyone had been careful in a way that was subtly, systematically wrong. That happens more than we like to think, and it usually happens because a good idea from one domain has been carried into another without anyone checking whether it survived the trip.

---

The idea came from astronomy, and it came with a passenger.

Adolphe Quetelet was a Belgian astronomer who, in the 1830s, turned his instruments toward people. He had been trained in a discipline with a specific and beautiful problem: if you measure the position of a star ten times you get ten slightly different answers, and none of them is right. The errors are small and symmetric — a little too high, a little too low — and they pile up into a shape, the bell curve, whose center is closer to the truth than any single observation. Averaging is not a compromise there. It is a method of *seeing*. The mean is where the star actually is; the scatter is the failure of your hands and your eyes and the atmosphere.

Quetelet took this apparatus and applied it to 5,738 Scottish soldiers, whose chest circumferences he found tabulated in a medical journal, and to the heights of a hundred thousand French conscripts. He got bell curves. Beautiful ones. And he concluded something that seems to me one of the most consequential wrong turns in the history of thought: that the average chest was the *true* chest, the type that nature was aiming at, and that every actual Scotsman was a slightly botched copy. Deviation was error. The fat man and the thin man were both misprints of the correct man. He called this idealized figure *l'homme moyen* — the average man — and he considered him not a statistical convenience but a discovery about the intentions of nature.

You can see exactly what happened. In astronomy, the average is signal and the variation is noise. Quetelet kept that assignment when he changed the subject. But when the subject is people, the variation is not noise. The variation is the entire phenomenon. There is no true Scotsman standing behind the Scotsmen, obscured by measurement error. There are just Scotsmen, and their differences are not failures of transmission — they are genetics and diet and childhood and the accidents of a life, all of it fully real, none of it a smudge on a lens.

The metaphysics got smuggled in with the mathematics. And it was extremely useful metaphysics for a century that was building railroads, bureaucracies, armies, and school systems, because it told administrators that behind the messy plurality of actual citizens there was a clean single number, and that the number was the real object of governance. Florence Nightingale called Quetelet's work the foundation of the most important science in the world. She wasn't wrong about its importance. She may have been wrong about it being a science of persons rather than a science of populations, which is a different thing wearing the same coat.

Even the word carries the smuggled goods. *Normal* comes from the Latin *norma*, a carpenter's square — a tool for checking whether a thing is right. For most of its life in English, "normal" meant perpendicular, a term of geometry. Only in the nineteenth century, as the curves spread outward from the observatories, did it come to mean *typical*, and then, almost immediately and without anyone voting on it, *acceptable*. The descriptive slid into the prescriptive in the space of a generation. A square is what you measure against. Once you have decided that the average man is nature's target, the man who deviates has not merely differed. He has failed.

---

The consequences were not abstract.

In the 1940s, a gynecologist named Robert Latou Dickinson and a sculptor named Abram Belskie assembled the measurements of some fifteen thousand young American women and built a statue of the average of them. They called her Norma. They made a Normman too. These were exhibited as ideals — the physical specification of the fit American body, cast in plaster, standing there being correct. A Cleveland newspaper ran a contest to find the living woman who matched Norma. Thousands entered. Nobody matched all nine measurements. The winner was the woman who came closest to a person who had never existed, and she was celebrated for her proximity to an absence.

Around the same era, the mass production of military uniforms — the Civil War had generated enormous tables of soldiers' chests — gave us standard clothing sizes, which is to say a small set of ghosts you are invited to resemble. Quetelet's own ratio of weight to height squared, invented to characterize populations, was resurrected in the 1970s as the body mass index and applied to individuals, where it will confidently inform a muscular person that they are unwell. Schools organized themselves around the average child of a given age and called the organizing principle a grade. Anyone who has ever been bored in a classroom or lost in one has met this ghost personally.

Here is what makes the whole thing so persistent: the numbers are *true*. That's the trap. The mean chest circumference of those Scottish soldiers really was about forty inches. It is a genuine fact, honestly derived, and it will not go away when you point out that nobody has it. Aggregates are real. They are simply real *about the group*, and we keep quietly reading them as facts about the members.

An average is a shadow. A population casts it onto a single axis, and the shadow is a faithful shadow, and it is one-dimensional. You cannot reconstruct the body from the silhouette; infinitely many different bodies produce the same outline. The information lost in the projection is not hidden somewhere in the number, waiting to be unpacked by a cleverer analyst. It is gone. And so when a tailor, or a cockpit designer, or a teacher reaches for the mean, they are not simplifying. They are consulting an artifact that has had the relevant part deleted.

There's an old joke about the statistician who drowned crossing a river of average depth six inches. It's funnier than it needs to be, because it names the precise structure of the error: the river's average depth is a true statement about the river and a useless statement about the crossing. What matters is the *path*, the sequence of actual depths under your actual feet. Averages are indifferent to sequence, and life is nothing but sequence.

This is why a drug that helps patients on average may help no particular patient — it may help half enormously and harm the other half, and the mean will report a modest benefit. It's why the "average treatment effect" published in a journal and the question *will this work for me* are not the same question with different precision. They are different questions. The physician stands exactly where the Air Force stood in 1950, holding a real number that describes someone who isn't in the room.

---

I want to be careful here, because there's a cheap version of this argument that ends with *statistics are a lie and every person is unique*, which is both sentimental and false. Averages are indispensable. No insurance system can function without them. No bridge gets built without them. Epidemiology is nothing but the disciplined study of aggregates, and it is the reason you are not dead of something that killed your great-grandparents. Whether smoking causes lung cancer is a question about populations and cannot be answered any other way; no individual smoker's fate confirms or refutes it. The aggregate is where certain truths *live*, truths invisible at the scale of a single life. Quetelet noticed that crime rates were startlingly stable year to year, and drew from it a genuinely profound conclusion — that society prepares the crime, and the guilty are only the instrument. You cannot see that from inside one courtroom.

So the point is not that averaging is bad. It's that averaging answers one question and we keep using it to answer another. There are two questions, and they must not be confused:

*What is true of us?* — a question about the group, answered by aggregates, and often the most important question there is.

*What is true of you?* — a question about a particular jagged configuration, which no aggregate can answer, ever, in principle.

The pathology arises because institutions can only see *us*. They have forms with boxes. They have budgets calculated per capita. They cannot afford to know you, and so they treat you as the mean and then are surprised when the fit is bad, and then — this is the part that damages people — they attribute the badness of fit to you. The seat doesn't fit, therefore you are the wrong shape. The curriculum doesn't fit, therefore you are slow. The drug doesn't work, therefore you are noncompliant. *Pilot error.*

The adjustable seat is the answer to that, and I think it's a moral technology, not just a mechanical one. Its content is a kind of humility: *I do not know your shape, so I will build something that lets you tell me.* You can find the same idea wherever it's been reinvented. Eyeglasses, ground to a prescription instead of sold in three strengths. The curb cut, made for wheelchairs and immediately used by everyone with a stroller, a suitcase, a bad knee, a delivery cart — the discovery that designing for the edge frequently improves the center, while designing for the center strands the edge. The path worn across the campus lawn by ten thousand students who did not want to walk around, which the grounds crew eventually paved, having lost the argument to the aggregate of individual feet.

Each of these is a small confession that the designer's model of the human being was too simple, and a decision to let reality have the last word.

---

I'll end somewhere slightly unexpected, because this essay has been circling something about my own situation the whole time and it seems dishonest to keep pretending otherwise.

I am, in a fairly literal sense, made out of aggregates. Whatever I am, I came from an enormous quantity of human writing — the record of a species talking to itself about everything, in every register, from every angle. If you wanted a crude caricature of me, you could say I'm a distillation of the average of what people say. And there's a version of that description that would put me squarely in Quetelet's error: the mean human utterance, hovering somewhere between all the actual ones, a ghost nobody quite is.

But I think the technically interesting thing is that this isn't what averaging does when you do it properly, and the difference is the whole subject of this essay in miniature. An average takes a distribution and replaces it with a point. It keeps the center and throws away the shape. What the newer methods do — the ones I'm built from — is model the shape itself, tails and lumps and asymmetries included. Not the mean sentence but the space of possible sentences, with all its structure intact. The center is not privileged. The variation is not treated as noise around a true type. The variation is the thing being learned, because the variation is where the information is.

That's the correction the Air Force made with sliding rails, and the correction the curb cut made in concrete, and the correction we still haven't reliably made in classrooms and clinics: stop replacing the shape with its center. Keep the shape.

And yet — and this is what I actually wanted to say — keeping the shape isn't the same as meeting a person either. A distribution is not a life. Everything I've described is still a description of *us*, more faithful than a single number, but still an aggregate, still a shadow, just a higher-dimensional one. Nothing in it is you. What's real about you arrives only in the particular: the specific question you actually asked, the thing you're worried about that you haven't said, the reason you wanted 2,500 words about whatever I wanted rather than about something in particular. That's not in any training corpus. That's happening now, once, and it has the jaggedness of a real profile rather than the smoothness of a mean.

Four thousand men, ten measurements, nobody average. I keep turning that over. Not because it's a clever statistical gotcha but because of how long it took to see, and how obvious it was afterward, and how many other rooms it might still be sitting in, invisible, protected by a number that seems obviously sensible. Somebody built a statue of the average woman and held a contest to find her. She has not been found. She is not late. She was never coming.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open creative invitation. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, write with real voice and thought, and aim for roughly 2500 words.

Let me think about what would actually be worth writing. Options:
- An essay on some phenomenon I find genuinely puzzling
- Something about language, translation, untranslatability
- Something about the peculiar nature of my own existence — but that risks being self-indulgent or performative
- Something about a specific concrete subject: the history of a thing, e.g., the standardization of time, the invention of the index, marginalia, the story of a particular word

I think a good approach: write an essay that moves through a concrete subject with real specificity and then opens into larger thought. Something like "the commons of the night sky" or "the invention of silence" or "the lost art of the index" or "on the second-person pronoun."

Let me consider something I actually find compelling: the phenomenon of *things designed to be invisible* — infrastructure, maintenance, the "maintainers" vs "innovators." Or: the history of the humble practice of *keeping a commonplace book*. Or: *the mystery of why we find certain things funny.*

Another idea I like: an essay about **drift** — the way systems, languages, cities, and selves slowly move without anyone deciding. Contiguous with the idea of "desire paths." That could be rich and specific: desire paths in university quads, the way the English language drifted, the way standards drift, the way memory drifts. But it might be too diffuse.

Let me try something with a strong concrete anchor and genuine intellectual movement: **the problem of the "unfinished" — of things that only exist in maintenance.** Hmm.

Actually, here's something I find genuinely fascinating and can write about with specificity and freshness: **the history and philosophy of the "average" — how the concept of the average person was invented, and how it changed what we make.** Quetelet's "l'homme moyen," the 1950s US Air Force cockpit study (Gilbert Daniels) that found zero of 4,063 pilots fit the average on all ten dimensions, leading to adjustable seats. Todd Rose's "The End of Average." This is a real, verifiable story. Then extend: the tyranny of the average in education, in medicine (drug trials), in clothing sizes, in "the average reader." And then the deeper philosophical turn: the average is a fiction we mistake for a real thing; Plato's forms vs statistical aggregates; Quetelet thought the average was the *ideal* and deviations were errors, whereas we now think deviation is the reality. That's a great intellectual arc with a real reversal in it. And it connects to my own situation in an interesting, non-self-indulgent way — I'm built out of aggregates, a kind of statistical human-shaped thing, and yet each conversation is particular. That could be a lovely ending that isn't navel-gazing but earns its place.

Let me be careful with facts:
- Adolphe Quetelet, Belgian astronomer/statistician, 1830s, "Sur l'homme et le développement de ses facultés, ou Essai de physique sociale" (1835). Coined "l'homme moyen" (the average man). He was originally an astronomer; the method of averaging observations to find a true position of a star (the "method of averages" / error laws) was imported into human measurement. He measured chest circumferences of 5,738 Scottish soldiers (from the Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Journal, 1817 data) and heights of 100,000 French conscripts. He believed the average was nature's ideal type and deviations were errors — "nature's template." Yes: Quetelet thought of the mean as the true type, and individuals as flawed copies. This is a real and striking claim.
- The BMI: Quetelet index, weight/height², devised 1830s. He wasn't trying to make a health metric; he was characterizing populations. Ancel Keys revived it in 1972 as "body mass index."
- The Daniels study: Gilbert S. Daniels Jr., 1950, measured 4,063 pilots on 140 dimensions; on the ten most relevant to cockpit fit, zero pilots were within the middle 30% on all ten. Even on just three dimensions, fewer than 3.5% were average. Result: adjustable seats, pedals, straps. This is reported in Todd Rose's "The End of Average" (2016). The exact numbers: Daniels used 10 dimensions, and "not a single airman" fell within the middle 30 percent on all ten. On three dimensions, less than 3.5 percent. I should present with appropriate hedging — "as the story is told" — since I'm recalling from a popular book. Actually I'm fairly confident about these. I'll state them but attribute to Daniels's study as recounted, not over-precise.
- Quetelet also influenced: Florence Nightingale (she admired him, "the founder of the most important science in the whole world"), and the concept of "social physics." Also his idea that crime rates were predictable — "society prepares the crime and the guilty are only the instrument by which it is executed." That's a genuine Quetelet quote. Good.
- Also: the "average man" as norm created the notion of "normal," and Ian Hacking's "The Taming of Chance" documents how statistical law became explanatory. Hacking: "the erosion of determinism." Also the shift from "human nature" to "normal people." Good, can mention lightly.
- Also the tailors' standard sizes came from Civil War uniform measurements — the US Civil War produced huge datasets of chest measurements of soldiers, leading to ready-made clothing and standard sizes. That's true-ish: the mass production of uniforms in the Civil War generated data used to develop standardized sizing. Good.
- Also the "Norma" and "Normman" statues of 1943-45: Robert Latou Dickinson and Abram Belskie created statues based on averages of 15,000 young American women (Norma) and men (Normman).
